subproblem.title: Cauchy–Schwarz bound for the normal excess on a set of finite measure: ∫_S |ν − e| dμ ≤ μ(S)·(2(1 − average of ⟨ν, e⟩ over S))^{1/2} (Simon (2); parent Steps 3 and 7)
subproblem.statement: Let N ∈ ℕ, μ a measure on ℝ^N, ν : ℝ^N → ℝ^N μ-a.e. strongly measurable with |ν| = 1 μ-a.e., e ∈ ℝ^N with |e| = 1, and S ⊆ ℝ^N any set with μ(S) < ∞. Put m := μ(S).toReal and I := ∫_S ⟨ν(y), e⟩ dμ(y). Then ∫_S |ν(y) − e| dμ(y) ≤ m · √(2(1 − m⁻¹ I)), where √ = Real.sqrt and m⁻¹ := 0 when m = 0.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (N : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Rn N)) (ν : Rn N → Rn N) (e : Rn N) (S : Set (Rn N)), μ S < ∞ → AEStronglyMeasurable ν μ → (∀ᵐ y ∂μ, ‖ν y‖ = 1) → ‖e‖ = 1 → ∫ y in S, ‖ν y - e‖ ∂μ ≤ (μ S).toReal * Real.sqrt (2 * (1 - (μ S).toReal⁻¹ * ∫ y in S, inner ℝ (ν y) e ∂μ))
subproblem.natural_proof:
(Implementation note: AEStronglyMeasurable.inner / AEStronglyMeasurable.inner_const live in Mathlib.MeasureTheory.Function.StronglyMeasurable.Inner, which is not in the import closure of GMT.Ch03.Submission and must be imported by the proof file.)
Source: parent proof Steps 3 and 7 (Simon Ch. 3, proof of Theorem 4.3, display (2), chapter-03.txt lines 615-620: since |ν| = 1, the averages of |ν − ν_E(x)| over B_ρ tend to 0), stated for an arbitrary set S of finite measure in place of B_ρ(x). Notation: μ_S := μ restricted to S (S need not be measurable: μ_S(ℝ^N) = μ(S) for every set S); every ∫_S below is an integral with respect to μ_S; m := μ(S).toReal; I := ∫_S ⟨ν(y), e⟩ dμ(y); J := ∫_S |ν(y) − e| dμ(y); K := ∫_S |ν(y) − e|² dμ(y); √ is Real.sqrt.

1. (Finite measure and a.e. facts.) Since μ(S) < ∞, μ_S is a finite measure with total mass μ(S); hence m is the real total mass of μ_S and ∫_S c dμ = c·m for every real constant c. Because μ_S is absolutely continuous with respect to μ, |ν| = 1 holds μ_S-a.e., and ν is μ_S-a.e. strongly measurable.

2. (Integrability; parent Step 3.) The functions f(y) := |ν(y) − e|, f(y)², and g(y) := ⟨ν(y), e⟩ are μ_S-a.e. strongly measurable, being continuous functions of ν. μ_S-a.e. they are bounded: |ν − e| ≤ |ν| + |e| = 2, so 0 ≤ f ≤ 2 and 0 ≤ f² ≤ 4; and |⟨ν, e⟩| ≤ |ν||e| = 1 (Cauchy–Schwarz in ℝ^N). An a.e.-bounded, a.e.-strongly-measurable function on a finite measure space is integrable, so f, f², g are μ_S-integrable.

3. (Pointwise identity and the value of K.) μ_S-a.e., |ν − e|² = |ν|² − 2⟨ν, e⟩ + |e|² = 1 − 2⟨ν, e⟩ + 1 = 2 − 2⟨ν, e⟩. Integrating over S (the two sides agree μ_S-a.e.; linearity of the integral, step 2, and ∫_S 2 dμ = 2m): K = 2m − 2I = 2(m − I).

4. (Case m = 0.) Since μ(S) < ∞, μ(S).toReal = 0 forces μ(S) = 0. Then μ_S is the zero measure and J = 0. The right-hand side is m · √(…) = 0 · √(…) = 0. Hence J ≤ RHS (both are 0).

5. (Cauchy–Schwarz, case m > 0; parent Step 7.) We prove J² ≤ m·K. This is the Cauchy–Schwarz (Hölder with exponents 2 and 2) inequality applied to the functions 1 and f on the finite measure space (S, μ_S), as in the parent proof (Mathlib integral_mul_le_Lp_mul_Lq_of_nonneg); for completeness, here is a direct derivation. Put c := J/m. Pointwise (f − c)² ≥ 0, and (f − c)² = f² − 2c·f + c² is μ_S-integrable by step 2. By linearity of the integral and ∫_S c² dμ = c²·m,
 0 ≤ ∫_S (f − c)² dμ = K − 2c·J + c²·m = K − 2J²/m + J²/m = K − J²/m.
 Multiplying by m > 0 gives J² ≤ m·K, i.e. by step 3, J² ≤ 2m(m − I).

6. (Conclusion, case m > 0.) J ≥ 0 because f ≥ 0. Hence, by monotonicity of √ and step 5, J = √(J²) ≤ √(2m(m − I)). Since m ≠ 0, 2m(m − I) = m² · 2(1 − m⁻¹ I). Because m² ≥ 0, √(m² · t) = √(m²)·√t = m·√t for every real t (Real.sqrt_mul with non-negative first factor, and √(m²) = m as m > 0); moreover here t = 2(1 − m⁻¹I) = 2(m − I)/m ≥ J²/m² ≥ 0 by step 5, so the radicand is non-negative under any convention for √. Therefore J ≤ m·√(2(1 − m⁻¹ I)), i.e. ∫_S |ν(y) − e| dμ(y) ≤ μ(S).toReal · √(2(1 − μ(S).toReal⁻¹ ∫_S ⟨ν(y), e⟩ dμ(y))). ∎
proof_key_steps: μ_S := μ⌞S is a finite measure with real total mass m = μ(S).toReal; |ν| = 1 μ_S-a.e. and ν is μ_S-a.e. strongly measurable.
f = |ν − e|, f² and ⟨ν, e⟩ are μ_S-a.e. strongly measurable and μ_S-a.e. bounded by 2, 4 and 1, hence μ_S-integrable.
μ_S-a.e. |ν − e|² = 2 − 2⟨ν, e⟩, so K := ∫_S |ν − e|² dμ = 2(m − I) with I := ∫_S ⟨ν, e⟩ dμ.
If m = 0 then μ(S) = 0, so J := ∫_S |ν − e| dμ = 0 and both sides vanish.
If m > 0: 0 ≤ ∫_S (f − J/m)² dμ = K − J²/m, so J² ≤ mK = 2m(m − I) (Cauchy–Schwarz).

audit.reason: The exact arbitrary-set contract is proved, including nonmeasurable S and zero mass. Restriction preserves the a.e. hypotheses; finite mass and boundedness justify every integral expansion. The identity K = 2(m − I), the integrated nonnegative square, and the justified square-root factorization establish the claimed bound. The proof is complete and independent.

subproblem.title: Basic facts at a reduced-boundary point: x ∈ U, unit reduced normal, convergence of the normal averages to it, and positive mass at every scale (parent Steps 1 and 4)
subproblem.statement: Let N ∈ ℕ, U ⊆ ℝ^N, μ a measure on ℝ^N and ν : ℝ^N → ℝ^N (no further hypotheses). Let x ∈ reducedBoundary U μ ν and e := reducedNormal μ ν x = limUnder_{ρ↓0} normalAverage μ ν x ρ, where normalAverage μ ν x ρ = μ(B_ρ(x)).toReal⁻¹ • ∫_{B_ρ(x)} ν dμ. Then x ∈ U, |e| = 1, normalAverage μ ν x ρ → e as ρ ↓ 0 (along 𝓝[>] 0), and μ(B_ρ(x)) > 0 for every ρ > 0.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (N : ℕ) (U : Set (Rn N)) (μ : Measure (Rn N)) (ν : Rn N → Rn N), ∀ x ∈ reducedBoundary U μ ν, x ∈ U ∧ ‖reducedNormal μ ν x‖ = 1 ∧ Tendsto (normalAverage μ ν x) (𝓝[>] 0) (𝓝 (reducedNormal μ ν x)) ∧ ∀ ρ : ℝ, 0 < ρ → 0 < μ (Metric.ball x ρ)
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof Steps 1 and 4 (Simon Ch. 3, definition (4.2) of the reduced boundary and the definition of ν_E(x) in 4.3). Notation: B_ρ := B_ρ(x) = Metric.ball x ρ (open ball); A(ρ) := normalAverage μ ν x ρ = (μ(B_ρ)).toReal⁻¹ • ∫_{B_ρ} ν dμ (Lean conventions: (∞).toReal = 0 and 0⁻¹ = 0); e := reducedNormal μ ν x = limUnder (𝓝[>]0) A. No hypothesis on U, μ or ν is needed.

1. (Unfolding the definition.) By definition of reducedBoundary, x ∈ reducedBoundary U μ ν means: x ∈ U, and there is v ∈ ℝ^N with A(ρ) → v along 𝓝[>]0 and |v| = 1. In particular x ∈ U, which is the first conjunct.

2. (Uniqueness of the limit.) The filter 𝓝[>]0 on ℝ is non-trivial (each of its members contains an interval (0, δ) with δ > 0, which is non-empty; Mathlib instance for 𝓝[>] on ℝ), and ℝ^N = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin N) is a metric space, hence Hausdorff. Therefore a function has at most one limit along 𝓝[>]0, and since A → v we get limUnder (𝓝[>]0) A = v (Mathlib Filter.Tendsto.limUnder_eq; the Nonempty-instance argument of limUnder is a proposition, so it does not matter which instance the definition of reducedNormal uses). Hence e = v.

3. (Second and third conjuncts.) From e = v and step 1: |e| = |v| = 1, and A(ρ) → v = e along 𝓝[>]0.

4. (Positive mass at every scale.) Let ρ > 0 and suppose, for a contradiction, that μ(B_ρ) is not positive. Since measures take values in [0, ∞], this means μ(B_ρ) = 0. For every r ∈ (0, ρ) we have B_r ⊆ B_ρ (Metric.ball_subset_ball, as r ≤ ρ), hence μ(B_r) ≤ μ(B_ρ) = 0, i.e. μ(B_r) = 0. Then (μ(B_r)).toReal = 0, its inverse is 0 by the convention 0⁻¹ = 0, and A(r) = 0 • ∫_{B_r} ν dμ = 0. The interval (0, ρ) belongs to 𝓝[>]0 (Ioo_mem_nhdsGT, since 0 < ρ), so A is eventually equal to the constant function 0 along 𝓝[>]0, and therefore A(r) → 0 along 𝓝[>]0. By uniqueness of limits along the non-trivial filter 𝓝[>]0 in the Hausdorff space ℝ^N (step 2), applied to A → v and A → 0, we get v = 0, so |v| = 0 ≠ 1, contradicting step 1. Hence 0 < μ(B_ρ) for every ρ > 0, which is the fourth conjunct. ∎
proof_key_steps: Unfold membership in reducedBoundary: x ∈ U and normalAverage μ ν x → v along 𝓝[>]0 with |v| = 1.

𝓝[>]0 is non-trivial and ℝ^N is Hausdorff, so reducedNormal μ ν x = limUnder (𝓝[>]0) (normalAverage μ ν x) = v (Filter.Tendsto.limUnder_eq); hence |reducedNormal μ ν x| = 1 and normalAverage μ ν x → reducedNormal μ ν x.

If μ(B_ρ(x)) = 0 for some ρ > 0, then μ(B_r(x)) = 0 and normalAverage μ ν x r = 0⁻¹ • (…) = 0 for all r ∈ (0, ρ) ∈ 𝓝[>]0, so normalAverage → 0, forcing v = 0, contradicting |v| = 1; hence μ(B_ρ(x)) > 0 for all ρ > 0.

audit.reason: Prose and one-line Lean proposition match without omitted hypotheses. The proof identifies reducedNormal with the unit limit using the nontrivial right-neighborhood filter, then obtains convergence and unit norm. Zero ball mass forces eventually zero averages, contradicting that unit limit. No child or parent theorem is assumed.

subproblem.title: The scalar normal averages μ(B_ρ(x))⁻¹ ∫_{B_ρ(x)} ⟨ν, ν_E(x)⟩ dμ tend to 1 at a reduced-boundary point (Simon (1); parent Steps 2, 3 and 5)
subproblem.statement: Let N ∈ ℕ, U ⊆ ℝ^N open, μ a measure on ℝ^N with μ(K) < ∞ for every compact K ⊆ U, and ν : ℝ^N → ℝ^N μ-a.e. strongly measurable with |ν| = 1 μ-a.e. Let x ∈ reducedBoundary U μ ν and e := reducedNormal μ ν x. Then μ(B_ρ(x)).toReal⁻¹ · ∫_{B_ρ(x)} ⟨ν(y), e⟩ dμ(y) → 1 as ρ ↓ 0 (along 𝓝[>] 0), with the Lean convention 0⁻¹ = 0.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (N : ℕ) (U : Set (Rn N)) (μ : Measure (Rn N)) (ν : Rn N → Rn N), IsOpen U → (∀ K : Set (Rn N), IsCompact K → K ⊆ U → μ K < ∞) → AEStronglyMeasurable ν μ → (∀ᵐ y ∂μ, ‖ν y‖ = 1) → ∀ x ∈ reducedBoundary U μ ν, Tendsto (fun ρ : ℝ ↦ (μ (Metric.ball x ρ)).toReal⁻¹ * ∫ y in Metric.ball x ρ, inner ℝ (ν y) (reducedNormal μ ν x) ∂μ) (𝓝[>] 0) (𝓝 1)
subproblem.natural_proof:
(Implementation note: integral_inner lives in Mathlib.MeasureTheory.Function.L2Space, which is not in the import closure of GMT.Ch03.Submission and must be imported; its form is ∫ ⟪c, f x⟫ ∂μ = ⟪c, ∫ f ∂μ⟫ (constant on the left), so combine it with real_inner_comm.)
Source: parent proof Steps 2, 3 and 5 (Simon Ch. 3, proof of Theorem 4.3, display (1), chapter-03.txt lines 607-614: lim_{ρ↓0} ∫_{B_ρ} ν·ν_E(x) dμ_E / μ_E(B_ρ) = 1). Notation: B_ρ := B_ρ(x) (open ball), B̄_ρ := closed ball, m_ℝ(ρ) := μ(B_ρ).toReal, A(ρ) := normalAverage μ ν x ρ = m_ℝ(ρ)⁻¹ • ∫_{B_ρ} ν dμ (Lean convention 0⁻¹ = 0), e := reducedNormal μ ν x, a(ρ) := m_ℝ(ρ)⁻¹ · ∫_{B_ρ} ⟨ν(y), e⟩ dμ(y).

1. (Sibling reduced_boundary_basic.) Applied to N, U, μ, ν and x ∈ reducedBoundary U μ ν, it gives x ∈ U, |e| = 1, and A(ρ) → e along 𝓝[>]0.

2. (A good closed ball; parent Step 2.) U is open and x ∈ U, so there is ε > 0 with B_ε ⊆ U. Put r := ε/2 > 0; then B̄_r ⊆ B_ε ⊆ U (as r < ε). The closed ball B̄_r is compact (ℝ^N is a finite-dimensional normed space, hence proper), so μ(B̄_r) < ∞ by the hypothesis on μ. For ρ ∈ (0, r) we have B_ρ ⊆ B̄_r, so μ(B_ρ) ≤ μ(B̄_r) < ∞.

3. (Integrability; parent Step 3.) Fix ρ ∈ (0, r). The restricted measure μ⌞B_ρ is finite by step 2. Because μ⌞B_ρ is absolutely continuous with respect to μ, ν is μ⌞B_ρ-a.e. strongly measurable and |ν| = 1 μ⌞B_ρ-a.e., so |ν| ≤ 1 μ⌞B_ρ-a.e. A bounded a.e.-strongly-measurable function on a finite measure space is integrable, so ν is μ⌞B_ρ-integrable.

4. (The inner product commutes with the integral; parent Step 5.) Fix ρ ∈ (0, r). The map w ↦ ⟨e, w⟩ is a continuous linear functional on ℝ^N, so it commutes with the Bochner integral of the μ⌞B_ρ-integrable function ν (Mathlib integral_inner): ∫_{B_ρ} ⟨e, ν(y)⟩ dμ(y) = ⟨e, ∫_{B_ρ} ν dμ⟩. Using the symmetry of the real inner product and ⟨t•w, e⟩ = t⟨w, e⟩ for t ∈ ℝ:
 ⟨A(ρ), e⟩ = m_ℝ(ρ)⁻¹ · ⟨∫_{B_ρ} ν dμ, e⟩ = m_ℝ(ρ)⁻¹ · ∫_{B_ρ} ⟨ν(y), e⟩ dμ(y) = a(ρ).
 (This holds for every ρ ∈ (0, r), whatever the value of m_ℝ(ρ), including m_ℝ(ρ) = 0 where both sides are 0.)

5. (Limit of the inner products.) The inner product ℝ^N × ℝ^N → ℝ is continuous, so A(ρ) → e (step 1) implies ⟨A(ρ), e⟩ → ⟨e, e⟩ = |e|² = 1² = 1 along 𝓝[>]0.

6. (Conclusion.) The interval (0, r) belongs to 𝓝[>]0 (since r > 0), and a(ρ) = ⟨A(ρ), e⟩ for all ρ in it (step 4). Hence a is eventually equal along 𝓝[>]0 to ρ ↦ ⟨A(ρ), e⟩, and by step 5, a(ρ) → 1 along 𝓝[>]0, i.e. μ(B_ρ(x)).toReal⁻¹ · ∫_{B_ρ(x)} ⟨ν(y), reducedNormal μ ν x⟩ dμ(y) → 1 as ρ ↓ 0. ∎
proof_key_steps: Sibling reduced_boundary_basic: x ∈ U, |e| = 1 and normalAverage μ ν x → e along 𝓝[>]0, where e = reducedNormal μ ν x.
Choose r > 0 with B̄_r(x) ⊆ U; compactness gives μ(B̄_r(x)) < ∞, hence μ(B_ρ(x)) < ∞ for ρ ∈ (0, r).
For ρ ∈ (0, r), ν is integrable on B_ρ(x) (a.e. strongly measurable, |ν| ≤ 1 a.e., finite measure).
integral_inner and real_inner_smul_left give ⟨normalAverage μ ν x ρ, e⟩ = μ(B_ρ).toReal⁻¹ ∫_{B_ρ} ⟨ν, e⟩ dμ for ρ ∈ (0, r).
⟨normalAverage μ ν x ρ, e⟩ → ⟨e, e⟩ = |e|² = 1 by continuity of the inner product; eventual equality on (0, r) ∈ 𝓝[>]0 transfers the limit.

audit.reason: All prose hypotheses appear exactly in the Lean proposition. The proof uses only its declared sibling dependency: openness and compact finiteness give integrability on sufficiently small balls; integral_inner and real symmetry identify the scalar averages; continuity and eventual equality give limit 1. The dependency reduced_boundary_basic → inner_average_limit is correctly directed and acyclic.
